title: Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) Technician (GySgt to LCpl) NMOS (2831, 2862), DIR IC4
raw_text:
4. MOS 2834, Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) Technician (GySgt to
LCpl) NMOS (2831, 2862), DIR IC4

    a. Summary. The Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) Technician MOS
identifies maintenance personnel that have received training to repair and



                                           3-253                        Enclosure (1)
 3124                                                                NAVMC 1200.1L



support the AEHF satellite communications system, Secure Mobile Anti-Jam
Reliable Tactical Terminal (SMART-T). Typical duties include tuning and
aligning systems, adjusting audio or data levels, using test equipment to
make checks on circuit quality, diagnosing equipment faults to the component
level, and replacing faulty parts or components. These Marines, submit field
service requests, conduct technical research and order repair parts to
restore system to operational status, and assist in the employment and
installation of the terminals within system capabilities. Marines in this
MOS may be assigned to a BIC (within their occupational field) that has been
coded with one or more DoD Cyber Workforce Framework (DCWF) work role codes.
Please reference DoDI 8140.10, DoDM 8140.10, and the MOS roadmap for
additional training and certification requirements associated with these work
role codes. This MOS will only be assigned to Marines holding primary MOS
2831 or 2862 and that are assigned to Division Communications Company or
Communications Battalion in support of this critical low density system.

       b.   Prerequisites

            (1) Must hold PMOS 2831 or 2862.

            (2) Security requirement:   secret security clearance eligibility.

       c.   Requirements

        (1) Complete the Digital Wideband Technician Course (DWTC) (A09DPG1),
Ft Gordon, GA.

        (2) Marines must have 12 months obligated service remaining upon
graduation from the Digital Wideband Technician Course. This obligated
service must be obtained prior to execution of TEMINS (DUINS) or TAD (DUINS)
orders to the course.

    d. Duties. For a complete listing of duties and tasks, refer to the
2800 Ground Electronics Maintenance Training and Readiness Manual.

    e. Related Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) Title and Code.
Radio Mechanics 49-2021.

       f.   Related Military Skill

            (1) Digital Wideband Systems Maintainer, 2831.

            (2) Ground Electronics Systems Maintenance Technician, 2862.
common_text: The Ground Electronics Maintenance Occupational Field includes the installation, inspection and classification, servicing, adjustment, tuning, repair, modification, recovery and evacuation, overhauling and rebuilding, and testing and calibration of electronic equipment and systems used by Marine Corps ground forces. The equipment includes various types of communications transmission systems, information technology systems, intelligence processing systems, tactical sensor systems, cryptographic devices, artillery electronics systems, digital fire control systems, unmanned vessel electronics, miscellaneous non-communication systems, robotic and various electro-mechanical systems, electronic jamming systems, and a wide range of test equipment and calibration required devices. Qualifications to work in this field include manual dexterity, normal color vision, be eligible to hold a secret security clearance, the ability to understand highly technical material, and to comprehend complex mathematical and logic principles. Types of entry-level jobs available include work as a Ground Electronics Transmission Systems Maintainer, Ground Electronics Telecommunications and Information Technology Systems Maintainer, Calibration Technician, Artillery Electronics Technician, and Digital Wideband Systems Maintainer. Formal schooling is provided to all Marines entering this field. In general, entry-level training consists of basic electronics, electronic systems fundamentals, and an equipment-oriented phase at either a Marine Corps school or other service school. Career progression training will involve related supervisory/technical level training within the field. Skill progression, skill enhancement and skill sustainment training is provided via on the job training and through both distributed learning and formal schooling. Billets for ground electronics maintenance are found throughout the Marine Corps but are concentrated within units having specific electronic or service support missions. Marines in this field may serve within GCE, ACE, MLG, MIG units and supporting establishments. Instructor billets are found at the formal schools responsible for ground electronics training. Marines entering this field will be assigned MOS 2800, Basic Ground Electronics Maintenance Marine.

matches: Modify, maintain, or repair electronics equipment or systems to ensure proper functioning.

The Ground Electronics Maintenance Occupational Field includes the installation, inspection and classification, servicing, adjustment, tuning, repair, modification, recovery and evacuation, overhauling and rebuilding, and testing and calibration of electronic equipment and systems used by Marine Corps ground forces.

Types of entry-level jobs available include work as a Ground Electronics Transmission Systems Maintainer, Ground Electronics Telecommunications and Information Technology Systems Maintainer, Calibration Technician, Artillery Electronics Technician, and Digital Wideband Systems Maintainer.
Supervise or train other technologists, technicians, or drafters.
Career progression training will involve related supervisory/technical level training within the field.
Install, service, and repair electronic equipment or instruments such as televisions, radios, and videocassette recorders.
Billets for ground electronics maintenance are found throughout the Marine Corps but are concentrated within units having specific electronic or service support missions.
Instructor billets are found at the formal schools responsible for ground electronics training.
Set up and operate specialized or standard test equipment to diagnose, test, or analyze the performance of electronic components, assemblies, or systems.

Typical duties include tuning and aligning systems, adjusting audio or data levels, using test equipment to make checks on circuit quality, diagnosing equipment faults to the component level, and replacing faulty parts or components.
Maintain and coordinate repair of marine machinery and equipment for installation on vessels.

These Marines, submit field service requests, conduct technical research and order repair parts to restore system to operational status, and assist in the employment and installation of the terminals within system capabilities.
Perform maintenance tasks necessary to keep equipment working properly.
For a complete listing of duties and tasks, refer to the 2800 Ground Electronics Maintenance Training and Readiness Manual.

nlx_method: NLx employer-demand profiles; private-only ownership unverified. Six-digit profiles pool specialty weighted task incidences after the existing review exclusion mask and five-job task-support floor; destination SOCs require 200 postings and nonzero tasks. Military profiles use binary accepted task presence and the same NLx reference RCA weights as civilian profiles: reciprocal positive task shares (zero weight for reference-absent tasks) of pooled retained support-five NLx weighted incidences across 1,016 reference specialties (912 eligible comparison candidates), sqrt(q * rca_weight), then L2 normalization and cosine. No military crosswalk codes enter the task ranking. All positive top-20 results retained; zero-similarity destinations are not recommendations. Shared field/rating duties are included; general Naval Standards remain separate by paygrade. Summary compares non-future individual source entries (versions can repeat) with nonempty reference sets; grouped, future and general-standard entries remain in all outputs. Hit@k is the fraction with at least one reference SOC recovered; ties are averaged exactly. References outside NLx remain in denominators. DMDC reference status is from July 2024, not current 2026 status.
